title: Reading Real-World Architectures
summary: Turn architecture write-ups into reusable patterns, and map interview prompts to practice.
keyPoints: Read an architecture post for user flows, data, bottlenecks, and trade-offs, not brand names.
Most large systems share an edge, stateless application, cache, database, queue, and worker skeleton.
Fan-out, consistent hashing, scatter-gather, and MapReduce solve different shapes of scale.
The seven rubric dimensions turn any architecture into a repeatable design conversation.
Object-oriented design questions are a separate interview format and are not covered here.

complexity.note: Trace one path before studying every box.
For offline jobs, not interactive requests.
Use the scenario checklist to review.

commonMistakes: Copying a company's diagram without its constraints, traffic profile, or trade-offs.
Memorizing product names instead of the problem each component solves.
Treating a fan-out write as free; it can turn one post into millions of writes.
Assuming scatter-gather is always faster without accounting for the slowest shard.
Claiming object-oriented design coverage because a scenario mentions classes.
interviewNotes: Open with one user flow and the read/write ratio.
Name the stateful components; they define the hard parts.
Map each component to a pattern and state its trade-off.
End with monitoring and what you would change at 10x.
Be explicit about topics you are not covering rather than bluffing.

checkYourself.question: Why does consistent hashing reduce cache misses when nodes change?
checkYourself.answer: Keys are mapped onto a ring, so adding or removing a node moves only the keys near that node instead of remapping nearly every key.

checkYourself.question: When is fan-out on write a poor choice?
checkYourself.answer: When one account has a very large number of followers. One write can become millions of feed writes, so a hybrid that merges celebrity posts at read time is often better.

checkYourself.question: What is the main latency risk in scatter-gather?
checkYourself.answer: The response waits for the slowest shard. A single slow or unavailable shard can dominate the tail latency.
